## 1. What was read

**637 research articles** from 32 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **292** records (31% of the 929 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

| General | Cancer | Immune | Bioinfo | Sysbio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 431 | 200 | 90 | 183 | 25 |

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: bioinfo -35%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). This month is missing *Nucleic Acids Res*. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: JAMA 113, Nature 71, Science 67, J Immunother Cancer 54, Nat Med 45, Nat Methods 41.

## 3. The evidence that moved it










**The divergence criterion was published as a title.**
[41372473](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41372473/) (*Nature Cancer*):
foundation models in oncology win benchmarks but miss the clinic. Every other
instance of this pattern in the corpus had to be assembled by putting an
enthusiastic preclinical block next to a negative or absent clinical one. Here
the journal states it. It is the single most useful card in the file, because it
is the only one where the reading and the finding are the same object.

**The virtual cell arrived as a Nature Methods title**
([41360943](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41360943/)), alongside
[Artificial intelligence agents for biology](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41360947/),
[Novae](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41372623/) and
[Nicheformer](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41168487/). The vocabulary, the
named models and the audits are in one journal in one month, which is the part
that can be read off the rows. No interval is quoted from the
[*Cell* Virtual Cell Challenge](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40578317/) any
more: the phrase was already a *Nature Biotechnology* title before that challenge
launched, so a span measured forward from it measures nothing.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-26"
    This paragraph first said *twelve* months, and the surrounding briefings
    said the virtual-cell vocabulary had not reached these journals before
    November. Both were wrong, and the error was one of sampling: each month's
    reader searched only its own month. The 2025-01..07 backfill found the
    phrase in [Nature Biotechnology in April 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40229360/),
    two months *before* the challenge that supposedly introduced it, and again
    in [*Cell* in August 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40713951/). The
    vocabulary did not arrive in December; it recurred, and the reason December
    looks like an arrival is that December is when it arrived in *Nature
    Methods* specifically.

**Agentic AI reached the immunology journals.**
[41348860](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41348860/) (*Sci Immunol*) is an
assessment commentary rather than a result, and it is the earliest
AI-as-discovery-agent framing in the nine immunology and systems-biology
journals *that this corpus has read* — which is not the same claim as the one
this paragraph used to make.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This paragraph carried a five-link dated chain — ESCARGOT on 4 February
    2025 as the first LLM-agent paper, the word *agentic* four days later,
    oncology in June, wet-lab-adjacent in August, immunology in December, and
    a "ten months, bench to bench" diffusion figure resting on all of it.

    Four of the five were already refuted by this corpus's own 2024 backfill
    and the paragraph was never updated. An LLM agent with tools is in a
    tracked journal in [2024-01](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38799228/),
    thirteen months before ESCARGOT, and an agent reaches an oncology journal
    in [2024-12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39690222/), six months before
    the date given here. The chain was wrong at its origin and at its oncology
    waypoint, so the interval computed from it was never a measurement of
    anything.

    The corrected version is not a better set of dates. It is that these are
    not datable from a bounded window at all — each "first" was the earliest
    month then being read. The corpus has now made this error six times.

**Checkpoints regressed to targets that are not checkpoints.** December's
nominations are CLEVER-1, CD300e, TIPE2 and NEAT1 — macrophage receptors and a
long non-coding RNA. Of August's roster, CD24 and TIM-3 survive; CD36, PYK2 and
ICOS are gone; TIGIT persists only as its ligand CD155. The only clinical-stage
non-PD-1 content is a B7-H3 review whose own title hedges
([41401407](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41401407/)) and an Fc-enhanced
CTLA-4 — both from waves preceding the current preclinical set. The category is
dissolving, not merely churning.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

Two *Nature Immunology* papers relocate CD47's relevant function from the
macrophage don't-eat-me axis to T-cell-intrinsic exhaustion via thrombospondin-1
([41258436](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41258436/),
[41249483](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41249483/)). Five months after two
negative CD47 phase 3s, this reads as a mechanistic post-mortem: the
phagocytosis-checkpoint rationale the programme was built on may have been the
wrong mechanism, not merely an under-powered one.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    [41423265](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41423265/) (*JITC*) was filed here
    as a refutation, on the argument that the safety carve-out in its title —
    "without inducing systemic toxicity" — was itself the finding: that systemic
    Treg depletion is understood to cause harm, and that the paper's selling
    point is avoiding it. That is carding a phrase in a title rather than a
    result in a paper, and the abstract attributes the systemic-toxicity problem
    to mogamulizumab, not to this agent.

    The study is a straightforwardly positive one. A tumour-targeted
    anti-HER2xCCR4 bispecific depletes tumour-infiltrating and tumour-chemotactic
    Tregs, raises the CD8/Treg ratio, controls advanced HER2-positive tumours in
    humanised mice without reducing Tregs systemically, and synergises with
    anti-PD-1. Depleting a suppressive population improved the outcome once the
    depletion was confined to the tumour, which is the thread's claim, and the
    card supports it.

    The question the paragraph went on to raise survives, and the corrected
    reading sharpens rather than weakens it. Read alongside
    [41401810](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41401810/) (*Immunity*, indexed
    2026-01), which reports opposing functions for distinct Treg subsets in
    colorectal cancer, what a depletion programme has to answer is not whether
    the population is suppressive but whether the marker it selects separates the
    subset that should go from the one that should stay. Confining the depletion
    to the tumour is one answer to that, and this paper is evidence that the
    answer works.

[41371211](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41371211/) is an *Immunity* preview of
Herbrich et al. in *Cancer Cell*, a paper this corpus does not hold: TET2-mutant
clonal haematopoiesis, an adverse host factor by assumption, reprograms tumour
macrophages and boosts checkpoint therapy. The inversion belongs on the thread;
the record carrying it is a commentary on another journal's work, which the
earlier version of this line did not say.

[41417925](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41417925/): Siglec-F+ neutrophils
promote resolution of lung injury.
[41272165](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41272165/): interferon-driven NK
activation raises cytolysis and lowers the neutralising antibody response — the
surrogate improves while the protective endpoint worsens, in one title.

### (b) Method credibility

[41331675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41331675/) (*Genome Biol*):
CRISPR-Cas9-induced double-strand breaks disrupt maintenance of epigenetic
information. Together with November's
[41196998](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41196998/), the two months say that
the most widely used perturbation in molecular biology corrupts the readout of
the field that uses it most.

The self-audit genre reached one paper in ten of the methods journals, its
highest share in the corpus, and its object escalated again — from the model, to
the pipeline, to the instrument
([41476115](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41476115/)), the wet-lab assay
(41331675), and the generative model's own output
([40523934](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40523934/), hallucination detection
in virtual staining). Auditing what a model emitted, rather than how it was
trained, is the newest object in the sequence — but it is not a new genre, and
this paragraph originally called it one. *Nature* audits a generative model's
own output in [2024-06](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38898292/), eighteen
months earlier. That correction was published in the 2024-06 briefing on
2026-08-26 and should have been applied here the same day; it was not.

[41102561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41102561/) (*Nat Med*) names a frontier
model and calls it brittle in medicine. In July the counterweight to clinical-AI
enthusiasm was opinion; it is now system-specific.

[41061703](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41061703/) (*Cell*): ascertainment, not
biology alone, produces the variable expressivity reported for complex
disorders.
[41344327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41344327/): retraction of the
transcriptome-scale Cas13 screen catalogue of essential lncRNAs.
[41327972](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41327972/): an Editor's Note attaches
to a foundational longitudinal ICB immune-signature and resistance paper.

**A hole in the month, recorded here so it is not read as biology.** *Nucleic
Acids Research* contributed zero rows to December; the `bioinfo` domain is 42%
below its median and the volume warning in section 1 fires on it. Everything
above about the methods journals is drawn from a month missing one of its
largest contributors, so the self-audit share of one in ten is computed on a
reduced denominator and is if anything an underestimate of the count.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-26"
    This paragraph called the hole a harvest defect, which implied it was
    ours and could be repaired by re-pulling. It cannot. Queried directly,
    PubMed returns **zero** *Nucleic Acids Research* research articles with a
    December 2025 publication date — the gap is in the source, not in the
    pull, and re-running the harvest reproduces it exactly. The
    denominator caveat above stands unchanged; the diagnosis does not.
    The same check found three more months that had been silently empty
    and would have read as quiet fields: *Bioinformatics* in 2024-04,
    2025-01, 2025-04 and 2026-03, and *Genome Research* in 2024-01. All
    return zero from PubMed too.

    Separately, and worse: *Nature Machine Intelligence* contributes **64
    papers to the entire 32-month corpus** and is absent from fifteen
    months of it, because PubMed indexes only its deposited fraction. It
    is a flagship venue for precisely the foundation-model and agentic-AI
    material these briefings track most closely. Every statement this
    corpus has made about where machine-learning methods are published is
    made with that venue effectively missing.
